clue.text: I give up drink permit

parts.note: a player who says 'pass' gives up their turn or chooses not to answer

explanation.surface: Someone swearing off alcohol, or perhaps refusing a drinks licence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I give up' reads as a statement by the speaker, but it is just what you say when you pass. 'Permit' looks like a verb in the surface; it is the noun at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A passport is an official travel document that authorises its holder to cross borders, a kind of permit.

clue.text: A little nipper toddling forward

indicators.note: only a small portion of the following words is wanted, a run of letters sitting inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A small child taking its first wobbly steps forward.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is in nipPER Toddling. 'Forward' looks like the toddler's direction of travel, but it means cheeky.
explanation.definitionFit: Forward in the sense of presumptuous or cheeky, and pert describes a bold, saucy manner.

clue.text: Place that article in centre of museum

indicators.note: one thing set in another goes inside it, so one piece sits within the other
the centre of a word is its middle letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of a six-letter word

explanation.surface: An instruction to a curator to put an exhibit in the middle of the museum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place' reads as an imperative verb, but it is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A site is a location or spot where something is or happens, the same as a place.

clue.text: Person investigating every tape I mixed

indicators.note: mixing a recording jumbles its parts, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A detective going through every recording that has been edited together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed' sounds like sound editing on a tape, which suits the investigator's evidence, but it signals the letters are scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: A private eye is an informal name for a private detective, someone hired to look into matters.

clue.text: Expose skin on remarkable calf

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so it comes first
the skin is the outer covering, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the word
veal is the meat of a calf

explanation.surface: Showing off the skin of a remarkable calf, as at a cattle show, or baring a shapely lower leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skin' looks like the thing being exposed, but it is the instruction to keep the outer letters. 'Calf' tempts the leg; here it is the animal, and its meat.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal something is to uncover it and make it visible, which is exactly what exposing does.

clue.text: Women's group backed by politician — he's wet

definitions.note: a phrase describing a person, standing for the noun

indicators.note: something backed by another has that other behind it, so that piece follows

parts.note: the WI is the Women's Institute, a community organisation in Britain and Canada
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A women's organisation endorsed by an MP, who is dismissed as feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed by' sounds like political support, but it only places the politician after the group. 'Wet' is British slang for feeble or ineffectual.
explanation.definitionFit: A wimp is a weak, timid person, and calling a man wet is British slang for exactly that feebleness.

clue.text: Screen it, after editing, behind closed doors

indicators.note: editing reworks material into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A film is shown privately once it has been cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screen' suggests showing a film, and editing fits the cinema picture, but the two words are just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Things done behind closed doors are kept private, away from public view, which is doing them secretly.

clue.text: Painting or paintings etc lifted through hole

indicators.note: one thing passing through another is surrounded by it, so it goes inside

parts.note: a pit is a hole in the ground

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting turns a word upward so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: art covers paintings and similar works

explanation.surface: Artworks being stolen through a hole in a gallery wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Painting or paintings' looks like a list, but 'or' is a piece of the answer. 'Lifted' sounds like theft; in a down clue it turns a word upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrait is a painting depicting a person, so it is a particular kind of painting.

clue.text: Fetch riveter nuts, last in crate

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it
nuts means crazy, so these letters are scrambled into a new order
the last of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

explanation.surface: A request to bring the riveter's nuts, the last of which are in a crate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like hardware a riveter would use, but it means crazy and signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrieve something is to go and get it back, which is what fetching means.

clue.text: Emperor's somewhat mordant, sarcastic

indicators.note: somewhat means to some degree, so only part of the following letters is used

parts.note: the letters bridge the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A ruler with a rather biting, scornful wit.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in mordanT SARcastic; the apostrophe-s is 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Tsar was the title of the Russian monarch, an absolute ruler of an empire.

clue.text: Carry On director might do this

definitions.text: Carry On director might do this

parts.words: Carry On director might do this
parts.note: surface reading: the director of a Carry On film shoots a part of the movie
setter's reading: to carry on is to cause a noisy fuss in public

explanation.walkthrough: The Carry On films are a long-running series of British comedy movies, so a director seems to be filming. Read 'carry on' as a verb and it means to kick up a fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a scene is an idiom for causing an embarrassing public fuss, and a film director also literally shoots scenes.

clue.text: Blemish on crazy Ottoman leader in country

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another is added after it

parts.note: an aga was a commander or chief officer in the Ottoman Empire
a scar is a mark left on the skin

explanation.surface: A stain on the record of a deranged Ottoman ruler somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ottoman leader' tempts you to take the first letter, O; here it is the title AGA. The blemish is written first but goes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Madagascar is an island nation off the southeast coast of Africa, an example of a country.

clue.text: Dog, one on a trampoline?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a breed of spaniel
second meaning, whimsical: someone who bounces up and down

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second meaning as playful: the noun is built from the verb to spring, so anyone leaping on a trampoline qualifies.
explanation.definitionFit: A springer spaniel is a gun dog breed, and literally a springer is anyone who jumps or leaps.

clue.text: Risotto prepared after first of martinis — and one for the road?

indicators.note: one thing after another is placed behind it in the answer
the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
food that is prepared has been worked on and changed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A meal cooked after a few martinis, plus a final drink before driving home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One for the road' is an idiom for a last drink before leaving, which fits the martinis; here it means a person who uses the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorist is a driver of a car, someone whose business is on the highway, so literally a road user.

clue.text: Bird heading for pigeon fancier

indicators.note: a heading is the top of something, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: a fancier is an enthusiast, one who loves something

explanation.surface: A bird flying home to its owner, someone who breeds pigeons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pigeon fancier' reads as one phrase, a pigeon keeper; split it and the bird gives only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The plover is a wading shorebird, one particular species within the broader class of birds.

clue.text: SW Asian troops and I behind you

indicators.note: what is behind another follows it, so those pieces come after

parts.note: ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: A commander tells an ally that his soldiers and he are backing them up in southwest Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind you' sounds like support, but it simply places the troops and I after YE.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yemeni comes from Yemen, a nation at the southwestern tip of the Arabian peninsula in Asia.

clue.text: Shocker after shocker in error

indicators.note: one thing after another follows it, so the two pieces sit side by side

explanation.surface: One scandal following another, through mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: A shocker usually means something dreadful; here it is the word you shout to make someone jump.
explanation.definitionFit: A boo-boo is an informal, childish word for a silly mistake or blunder.

clue.text: A victory so unlikely for country

indicators.note: something unlikely is improbable or out of order, so these letters will not stay as given

explanation.surface: A sporting nation's win was a real long shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unlikely' reads as a comment on the victory, but it signals the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivory Coast, also called Côte d'Ivoire, is a West African nation, one example of a country.

clue.text: A moggy bit!

parts.note: moggy is British slang for a cat

explanation.surface: An outraged report that a cat has bitten someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit' looks like the past tense of bite, the cat's crime; it is the noun meaning a tiny piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An atom is figuratively the smallest possible amount of something, a tiny fragment or speck.

clue.text: Cut when half-cut!

indicators.note: half-cut is slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger out of order

explanation.surface: A quip about a woodcutter, or a barber, working while tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' seems to echo the definition, half-way through a cut; it is British slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Hewn is the past participle of hew, to chop with an axe, so it means chopped or carved.

clue.text: Smooth surfaces on ground level in ballroom

indicators.note: a surface is the top layer, so the topmost, opening letters are kept

explanation.surface: Polished dance floors on the ground floor of a ballroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth surfaces' reads as a single phrase about floors; split it, and 'surfaces' is a verb-like signal to take tops of words.
explanation.definitionFit: Glib describes speech that is slick and fluent but shallow, one sense of smooth as applied to talkers.

clue.text: Mysterious beast e'en, one's nowhere to be seen

indicators.note: something mysterious is puzzling and obscure, so the letters are disguised in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A mysterious creature that comes out at evening, like a Yeti, which never shows itself.
explanation.walkthrough: E'en is the poetic contraction of evening (or even), which supplies the needed extra Es.
explanation.definitionFit: An absentee is a person who is missing from where they ought to be, someone not present.

clue.text: 9 going wrong, dammit!

indicators.note: anything going wrong falls out of its proper order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone cursing when a plan has failed.
explanation.walkthrough: The 9 refers to the solution of clue 9 across, an emperor; the exclamation is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rats is a mild exclamation of irritation or disappointment, used in place of a curse.

clue.text: Evil spirit — and poor golfer?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a frightening imaginary monster
second meaning, whimsical: a player who takes one over par on holes

explanation.walkthrough: In golf, a bogey is a score of one stroke over par on a hole, so a golfer who keeps making them is a BOGEY MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The bogeyman is a mythical creature used to frighten children, and literally a person who scores bogeys.
